lessons.title: Lesson 1: Introduction to Irrigation Systems in African Agriculture
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3 of the Agricultural Irrigation Technician course. In this first lesson, we lay the foundation for everything that follows by exploring why irrigation matters so much in Africa and what systems are commonly used across the continent. Agriculture remains the backbone of most African economies, employing over 60 percent of the labour force in many countries. Yet, only a small fraction of cultivated land is irrigated, leaving farmers at the mercy of erratic rainfall. As an irrigation technician, your role is to help bridge that gap by designing, installing, and maintaining systems that deliver water efficiently and reliably. We begin with the water cycle and soil-water relationships. Plants take up water through their roots, and that water must be replaced either by rain or irrigation. The amount of water a soil can hold depends on its texture. Sandy soils drain quickly and hold little water, while clay soils hold more but may become waterlogged. Loam soils are ideal. You will learn to estimate soil moisture using simple methods like the feel test or a soil moisture meter. Next, we survey the main irrigation methods used in Africa. Surface irrigation, including furrow and basin systems, is common in the Nile Delta, the Senegal River Valley, and parts of Zimbabwe. It is cheap but can waste water and cause erosion. Sprinkler irrigation, including hand-move, solid-set, and centre pivot systems, is used on commercial farms in South Africa, Kenya, and Zambia. It suits sandy soils and uneven terrain but requires pressure and energy. Drip irrigation, also called trickle irrigation, delivers water directly to the root zone through emitters. It is the most water-efficient method and is expanding rapidly in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Morocco, especially for high-value crops like vegetables and flowers. We also discuss the importance of water sources. In Africa, irrigation water comes from rivers, lakes, reservoirs, boreholes, and even treated wastewater. Each source has implications for water quality, pumping requirements, and legal rights. You must understand local water laws and permits. For example, in South Africa, the National Water Act requires registration for water use. In Kenya, the Water Resources Authority issues permits. As a technician, you will often work with smallholder farmers who cannot afford complex systems. Your challenge is to recommend affordable, appropriate technology. A treadle pump or a solar-powered drip kit may be more suitable than a diesel pump. We close this lesson by outlining the technician's responsibilities: assessing site conditions, measuring water flow, selecting pipes and fittings, installing pumps and filters, and training farmers on operation and maintenance. You are not just a mechanic; you are a business advisor who helps farmers increase yields and incomes. Remember that irrigation is not just about water; it is about timing, quantity, and uniformity. Over-irrigation wastes water and leaches nutrients, while under-irrigation stresses crops and reduces yields. Your goal is to apply the right amount at the right time. In the next lesson, we will dive into system components and design principles. Before you move on, complete the self-check questions at the end of this module. Ask yourself: What are the three main irrigation methods? What soil type holds the most water? Why is drip irrigation popular for vegetables? Write down your answers and review them. This lesson has given you a broad overview. In practice, you will need to adapt to local conditions. For instance, in the Sahel, where rainfall is scarce, you might promote rainwater harvesting combined with drip irrigation. In the highlands of Ethiopia, you might design gravity-fed systems from springs. In the lowlands of Mozambique, you might rehabilitate existing furrow systems. Always consider the farmer's budget, labour availability, and market access. A system that is not maintained is worse than no system at all. So, from the start, involve the farmer in decision-making and plan for spare parts. Now, let us move to the technical details. In the following lessons, you will learn how to measure water flow, calculate pump requirements, select pipes, install filters, and troubleshoot problems. You will also learn about fertigation, which is injecting fertiliser into irrigation water, a practice that is growing in Kenya and South Africa. By the end of this module, you should be able to design a simple drip system for a one-hectare vegetable plot, install a solar pump, and maintain a sprinkler system. You will also understand the economics of irrigation, including payback periods and return on investment. This is a practical course, so keep a notebook and take notes. Visit local farms and observe different systems. Talk to farmers about their challenges. The more you engage, the better technician you will become. Let us begin.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Components of an Irrigation System and Their Functions
lessons.body: In this lesson, we examine the hardware that makes irrigation possible. Every irrigation system, from a simple bucket drip kit to a large centre pivot, consists of several key components: water source, pump, power unit, mainline, submain, laterals, emitters or sprinklers, filters, valves, and controls. Understanding each component and how they work together is essential for installation, maintenance, and troubleshooting. We start with the water source. This could be a river, lake, dam, borehole, well, or tank. The source must provide enough water throughout the growing season. You need to measure the flow rate, usually in litres per second or cubic metres per hour. A simple method is the bucket and stopwatch: fill a 20-litre bucket and record the time. If it takes 10 seconds, the flow is 2 litres per second. For boreholes, you may need a pump test. Next is the pump. Pumps add energy to water to move it from the source to the field. The most common types in Africa are centrifugal pumps, submersible pumps, and positive displacement pumps like piston or diaphragm pumps. Centrifugal pumps are used for surface water and shallow wells. Submersible pumps are placed inside boreholes. Solar pumps are increasingly popular because they have no fuel costs. When selecting a pump, you need to know the total head, which is the sum of suction lift, discharge head, and friction losses. The pump must also match the flow rate required by the system. Power units include diesel engines, electric motors, and solar panels. Diesel is reliable but expensive to run. Electric motors are cheaper per hour but need grid connection. Solar is clean and free after installation but requires battery storage or direct drive during sunny hours. In many African countries, solar pumps are now cheaper than diesel over a five-year period. The mainline carries water from the pump to the field. It is usually made of PVC or galvanised steel and is buried underground to protect it from sunlight and damage. The submain distributes water to different sections of the field. Laterals are the pipes that carry water to the emitters or sprinklers. For drip systems, laterals are usually made of polyethylene and are laid on the soil surface or buried. Emitters are the devices that release water to the plants. In drip systems, emitters can be inline (built into the lateral) or online (attached to the lateral). They have different flow rates, typically 1 to 8 litres per hour. Sprinklers are used in sprinkler systems and can be impact, gear-driven, or spray types. Filters are critical, especially for drip irrigation. They remove sand, silt, and organic matter that can clog emitters. Common filters include sand separators, screen filters, and disc filters. A sand separator removes heavy particles, a screen filter catches fine debris, and a disc filter provides fine filtration. You must clean filters regularly. Valves control the flow of water. Gate valves are used for on/off control, while globe valves regulate flow. Check valves prevent backflow. Air release valves remove trapped air. Pressure regulators maintain constant pressure. Controls can be manual or automatic. Manual systems require a person to open and close valves. Automatic systems use timers or soil moisture sensors. In Africa, automatic systems are less common due to cost and unreliable electricity, but they are growing in commercial farms. We also discuss the importance of pressure. Most drip systems operate at 1 to 2 bar, while sprinklers need 2 to 4 bar. Pressure that is too high can damage pipes and emitters, while low pressure reduces uniformity. You will learn to use a pressure gauge and adjust the system accordingly. Another key component is the fertigation unit, which injects fertiliser into the irrigation water. This is common in greenhouses and high-value crops. Venturi injectors and dosing pumps are used. You must ensure that fertilisers are compatible and that the system is flushed after injection. Now, let us consider the layout of a typical drip system for a one-hectare plot. The water source is a borehole with a submersible pump. Water is pumped to a tank on a raised platform. From the tank, it flows by gravity through a mainline, then a submain, then laterals. A sand filter and screen filter are installed after the pump. A pressure regulator and a valve control each block. The laterals are spaced 1 metre apart, with emitters every 30 centimetres. This system can irrigate vegetables like tomatoes, kale, and onions. For a sprinkler system, the layout is similar but with sprinklers instead of emitters. You need to space sprinklers according to their wetted diameter and ensure overlapping. Wind can affect uniformity, so avoid irrigating during windy periods. Maintenance is a major part of your job. You will need to flush laterals, clean filters, check for leaks, and replace damaged emitters. Keep a maintenance log. Train farmers to do daily checks. A well-maintained system can last 10 to 15 years. In summary, an irrigation system is a chain of components, and the weakest link determines performance. Your task is to ensure every component is correctly sized, installed, and maintained. In the next lesson, we will focus on pump selection and installation. Before you move on, list the components of a drip system and describe the function of each. Then, visit a local farm and identify the components you see. This practical exercise will reinforce your learning.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Pump Selection, Installation, and Maintenance
lessons.body: Pumps are the heart of most irrigation systems. Without a properly selected and maintained pump, water will not reach your crops. In this lesson, we focus on pump types, how to calculate pump requirements, installation best practices, and maintenance routines. We begin with the basic principle: a pump moves water by creating a pressure difference. The energy required depends on the flow rate and the total head. Flow rate is the volume of water per unit time, usually litres per second or cubic metres per hour. Total head is the vertical lift plus friction losses in pipes and fittings. You must calculate both accurately. To calculate total head, you need to know the static lift, which is the vertical distance from the water surface to the highest point of discharge. If the pump is above the water surface, this is suction lift. If the pump is submerged, it is discharge head. Then add friction loss. Friction loss depends on pipe diameter, length, flow rate, and pipe material. You can use friction loss charts or online calculators. A common mistake is to undersize pipes, which increases friction and reduces flow. As a rule, keep water velocity below 1.5 metres per second in mainlines and below 1 metre per second in laterals. Now, let us look at pump types. Centrifugal pumps are the most common. They use a rotating impeller to push water. They are efficient for low to medium heads and high flows. They cannot self-prime, so you need a foot valve or a priming chamber. Submersible pumps are designed to be placed inside a borehole. They are multistage, meaning they have multiple impellers to achieve high heads. They are cooled by the water around them, so they must not run dry. Positive displacement pumps, such as piston and diaphragm pumps, are used for low flows and high heads. They are common in hand pumps and solar pumps. Solar pumps are either centrifugal or positive displacement. They use DC motors powered by photovoltaic panels. They are ideal for remote areas without grid electricity. When selecting a pump, you need a pump curve. This is a graph provided by the manufacturer showing the relationship between flow rate and head. You must select a pump whose curve passes through your required flow and head. The best efficiency point is where the pump operates most efficiently. Avoid operating far to the left or right of this point. Installation is critical. For surface pumps, place the pump as close to the water source as possible to reduce suction lift. Suction lift should not exceed 7 metres at sea level, and less at higher altitudes. Use a suction pipe that is at least as large as the pump inlet. Install a foot valve with a strainer to prevent debris from entering. For submersible pumps, ensure the borehole is straight and clean. Lower the pump gently using a safety rope. Install a non-return valve to prevent backflow. Connect the drop pipe, which can be galvanised steel or polyethylene. For solar pumps, mount the panels facing the equator at an angle equal to your latitude. Use a controller to match the pump to the solar array. Maintenance is essential. For diesel pumps, check oil, fuel, and air filters regularly. Clean the cooling fins. For electric pumps, check voltage and current. For solar pumps, clean panels weekly and check wiring. For all pumps, listen for unusual noises, check for leaks, and monitor flow rate. A drop in flow may indicate wear on the impeller or a clogged filter. You should also protect pumps from theft, which is a common problem in some African countries. Build a lockable cage or house the pump in a secure room. Now, let us work through an example. A farmer in Kenya wants to irrigate one hectare of tomatoes using drip irrigation. The water source is a borehole with a water level 20 metres below ground. The tank is 5 metres above ground. The total pipe length is 100 metres. The required flow is 10 cubic metres per hour. Calculate the total head. Static lift is 20 plus 5 equals 25 metres. Friction loss for 10 cubic metres per hour through a 50mm pipe over 100 metres is approximately 2 metres. Add fittings losses of 1 metre. Total head is 28 metres. Select a pump that delivers 10 cubic metres per hour at 28 metres head. A submersible pump with a 1.5 kilowatt motor would be suitable. For solar, you would need about 2 kilowatts of panels. This example shows how calculations guide selection. In practice, you may not have perfect data, so use conservative estimates. Always add a safety margin of 10 to 20 percent. Finally, consider the cost. A diesel pump may cost 500 USD but consume 2 litres of fuel per hour. At 1.5 USD per litre, that is 3 USD per hour. A solar pump may cost 2000 USD but have no fuel cost. Over 2000 hours of operation, diesel costs 6000 USD, while solar costs 2000 USD. So solar is cheaper in the long run. However, solar requires sun, so you may need a backup for cloudy days. In conclusion, pump selection is a technical and economic decision. You must balance capital cost, operating cost, reliability, and maintenance. Always involve the farmer in the decision. In the next lesson, we will cover water filtration and fertigation. Before you move on, practice calculating total head for a scenario in your area. Then, visit a local pump supplier and ask for pump curves. This will build your confidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Filtration, Fertigation, and Water Quality Management
lessons.body: Water quality is often overlooked in irrigation, but it can make or break a system. In this lesson, we cover filtration, fertigation, and management of water quality issues. We start with filtration. Filters protect emitters and sprinklers from clogging. Clogging is the number one cause of drip system failure. There are three main types of filters: sand separators, screen filters, and disc filters. Sand separators, also called hydrocyclones, use centrifugal force to remove sand and heavy particles. They are installed before the main filter. Screen filters use a mesh screen to catch fine particles. They are rated in mesh size, with higher numbers meaning finer filtration. For drip irrigation, a 120-mesh screen is common. Disc filters use stacked discs with grooves that trap particles. They are easy to clean and provide fine filtration. The selection of filters depends on water quality. If your water source is a river or canal, you need a sand separator followed by a screen or disc filter. If your water is from a borehole, it may be clean enough for a screen filter alone. Always install a filter after the pump and before the mainline. You also need to consider pressure loss across filters. A clogged filter causes pressure loss, which reduces emitter flow. Install pressure gauges before and after the filter. If the difference exceeds 0.5 bar, clean or replace the filter. Cleaning is simple: open the flush valve and rinse. For screen filters, remove the screen and brush it. For disc filters, open the housing and separate the discs. Do this weekly or more often if water is dirty. Now, let us discuss fertigation. Fertigation is the injection of fertiliser into irrigation water. It saves labour and ensures nutrients reach the root zone. It is common in greenhouses and for high-value crops like tomatoes, peppers, and flowers. The main methods are venturi injectors, dosing pumps, and pressure differential tanks. A venturi injector uses a pressure difference to suck fertiliser into the water. It is cheap but has a high pressure loss. A dosing pump is electric and precise but more expensive. A pressure differential tank is a simple tank that is connected across a valve. Fertigation requires careful management. First, ensure the fertiliser is fully soluble. Insoluble fertilisers will clog emitters. Second, inject fertiliser near the end of the irrigation cycle, then flush with clean water for 10 to 15 minutes. This prevents fertiliser from remaining in the laterals and causing algae or salt buildup. Third, never mix calcium with phosphate or sulphate fertilisers, as they form precipitates. Use separate tanks. Fourth, calibrate your injector regularly. You can use a simple method: inject a known amount of fertiliser and measure the concentration in the water. Water quality also affects irrigation. Salinity is a major issue in arid regions like the Sahel and parts of North Africa. High salinity reduces water uptake by plants and can cause leaf burn. You can measure salinity using an electrical conductivity meter. Most crops tolerate up to 2 decisiemens per metre, but some are more sensitive. If salinity is high, you may need to leach the soil with extra water. Another issue is sodium. High sodium can destroy soil structure, making it impermeable. You can add gypsum to remedy this. Iron and manganese can cause staining and clogging. They are common in borehole water. Aeration and filtration can remove them. Bacteria and algae can grow in warm, stagnant water. They clog emitters and filters. Keep water moving, cover tanks, and chlorinate if necessary. Chlorination is common in commercial systems. Use 1 to 2 parts per million of free chlorine. Be careful not to over-chlorinate, as it can damage plants. Now, let us consider a practical scenario. A farmer in Ethiopia uses a river to irrigate onions with drip. The water is muddy during the rainy season. The system clogs frequently. Your solution: install a sand separator and a disc filter. Clean the sand separator daily and the disc filter twice a week. Also, install a settling tank before the pump to allow heavy sediment to settle. This will reduce filter cleaning frequency. For fertigation, the farmer wants to apply NPK 20-10-10. You recommend a venturi injector because it is affordable. You teach the farmer to inject for 30 minutes, then flush for 15 minutes. You also advise using a separate tank for calcium nitrate. This scenario shows how filtration and fertigation go hand in hand. You must also consider the cost. A sand separator costs about 200 USD, a screen filter 50 USD, and a venturi injector 100 USD. These are small investments compared to the cost of replacing clogged emitters. In summary, filtration protects your system, fertigation feeds your crops, and water quality management ensures long-term success. As a technician, you must test water quality at the start of each season. Use a simple test kit for pH, salinity, and hardness. Keep records. Train farmers to monitor filters and flush laterals. In the next lesson, we will cover system design and layout. Before you move on, list three types of filters and describe when to use each. Then, calculate the dilution rate for a fertiliser if you want 100 grams per plant per week. This practical exercise will prepare you for real-world challenges.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: System Design, Layout, and Troubleshooting
lessons.body: In this final lesson of Module 3, we bring everything together by focusing on system design, layout, and troubleshooting. You will learn how to design a simple irrigation system from scratch, create a layout plan, and diagnose common problems. We start with the design process. The first step is to gather information: crop type, area, soil type, water source, flow rate, pressure, and farmer's budget. You also need to know the peak water requirement of the crop, which is the maximum amount of water the crop needs per day. This is usually given in millimetres per day. For example, tomatoes in a hot climate may need 6 millimetres per day. One millimetre over one hectare is 10 cubic metres of water. So, 6 millimetres is 60 cubic metres per day. If you irrigate for 4 hours, you need a flow rate of 15 cubic metres per hour. Next, you select the irrigation method. For vegetables, drip is best. For maize or wheat, sprinkler or surface may be more economical. For orchards, micro-sprinklers or drip are common. Then, you design the layout. For drip, you need to decide lateral spacing and emitter spacing. These depend on crop row spacing and soil type. For tomatoes planted in rows 1 metre apart, use one lateral per row. For onions planted in beds, use two laterals per bed. Emitter spacing is usually 30 centimetres for sandy soils and 40 to 50 centimetres for clay soils. You also need to decide the number of blocks. A block is a section that is irrigated at the same time. Dividing the field into blocks allows you to use a smaller pump and pipe. For example, a one-hectare field can be divided into four blocks of 0.25 hectares each. You irrigate one block at a time. This reduces the required flow rate by four times. Now, you calculate pipe sizes. The mainline must carry the total flow of the block. The submain carries flow to each lateral. Use friction loss charts to select diameters that keep velocity below 1.5 metres per second. For a 15 cubic metres per hour flow, a 63mm PVC pipe is suitable for the mainline. For laterals, 16mm polyethylene is standard. You also need to select the pump based on total head and flow. Then, you select filters, valves, and fittings. Create a bill of quantities with prices. This helps the farmer see the total cost. A typical drip system for one hectare in Kenya costs between 1500 and 3000 USD, depending on the source and quality. Now, let us discuss layout. Draw a map of the field to scale. Mark the water source, pump, tank, mainline, submain, and laterals. Show the position of filters, valves, and pressure regulators. Include a flush valve at the end of each lateral. This map is your installation guide. It also helps the farmer understand the system. During installation, follow the map. Lay out the mainline first, then the submain, then the laterals. Use a trencher or hand tools to bury the mainline. Keep laterals on the surface but secure them with pegs. Install emitters according to the spacing. Test each block for pressure and flow. Adjust the pressure regulator to the recommended level. Flush the system thoroughly before planting. Troubleshooting is a critical skill. Common problems include low pressure, uneven flow, clogged emitters, leaks, and pump failure. Low pressure can be caused by a clogged filter, a leak, or a worn pump. Check the pressure gauge at the pump and at the end of the mainline. If the difference is large, the filter is clogged. If pressure is low everywhere, the pump may be undersized or the water level may have dropped. Uneven flow can be caused by pressure differences along the lateral. This is more common in long laterals. Keep laterals shorter than 100 metres. Clogged emitters are usually due to dirty water or fertiliser precipitates. Remove the emitter and clean it or replace it. Leaks are caused by damaged pipes or fittings. Repair with a coupling or replace the section. Pump failure can be due to power supply, impeller wear, or airlock. Check the power first. For solar pumps, check the panels and controller. Airlock can be cleared by opening a valve at the highest point. You should also train farmers to do daily checks. They should look at the pressure gauge, check for leaks, and flush filters. They should keep a log of maintenance activities. A simple checklist can prevent major failures. Now, let us consider a case study. A farmer in Tanzania has a one-hectare drip system for kale. The system was installed two years ago. The farmer complains that the kale is wilting even though the pump runs. You visit the site. You check the pressure at the pump: 2 bar. At the end of the mainline: 0.5 bar. You suspect a clogged filter. You open the sand separator and find it full of sand. You clean it. Pressure returns to 1.8 bar. You also notice that some emitters are clogged. You flush the laterals and clean the emitters. You advise the farmer to clean the sand separator daily and flush laterals weekly. This simple fix saves the crop. In another case, a farmer in Nigeria has a sprinkler system that does not reach the edges of the field. You check the pump and find it is a centrifugal pump with a worn impeller. You replace the impeller. The system works again. These examples show that troubleshooting is about systematic checking. Always start from the source and work your way to the emitters. Use a pressure gauge and a flow meter. Keep spare parts. In conclusion, system design and troubleshooting are the core skills of an irrigation technician. You must be able to design a system that is efficient, affordable, and maintainable. You must also be able to diagnose and fix problems quickly. This module has given you the foundation. Practice by designing systems for different crops and fields. Visit farms and learn from experienced technicians. Remember that irrigation is a business. Your designs should help farmers increase yields and profits. In the next module, we will cover advanced topics like automation, soil moisture sensors, and climate-smart irrigation. Before you move on, complete the final assessment. Design a drip system for a 0.5-hectare tomato field with a borehole yielding 5 cubic metres per hour. Calculate the number of blocks, pipe sizes, and pump head. Then, list five troubleshooting steps for low pressure. This will test your understanding. Thank you for your attention. I wish you success in your work as an irrigation technician.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Field Data, Sizing Tables, and Safe Operating Limits for Irrigation Technicians in Africa

This Practical Reference lesson is the technician's bench book. It does not re-teach theory. It gives you the numbers, the conversions, the tolerances, and the safety rules you need on a farm in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia, Senegal, or Zambia when the pump is running, the client is watching, and the crop cannot wait. Use it alongside Lessons 1â5. Keep a printed copy in the service vehicle. Every figure here is traceable to a published source so you can defend your recommendation to a farmer, a cooperative, or a financier.

Business-first framing: an irrigation technician who can quote a defensible flow rate, pressure, and filtration spec closes more service contracts than one who only repairs breakdowns. Accurate field data reduces callbacks, protects your reputation, and turns one-off repairs into seasonal maintenance agreements. The tables below are designed to be used during a site visit, not after it.

Figure 1: Reference Layout of a Pressurized Drip Irrigation Block

How to use Table 1: Confirm the emitter flow rate at the actual operating pressure, not at the catalogue reference pressure. A 2.0 L/h emitter rated at 1.0 bar will deliver more or less than 2.0 L/h at 1.4 bar depending on its exponent (x). For turbulent-flow emitters, x â 0.5; for pressure-compensating emitters, x â 0. If your measured flow is more than 10% off the design value, check filtration, pressure, and emitter clogging before adjusting the schedule.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â WATER QUALITY, CHEMICALS, AND HUMAN HEALTH

Fertigation and chemigation inject fertilizers, acids, and pesticides into irrigation water. These chemicals can contaminate drinking water, burn skin and eyes, and cause acute poisoning. The following rules are non-negotiable:

  • Never inject chemicals upstream of a drinking-water take-off. Install a verified air gap or reduced-pressure-zone (RPZ) backflow preventer. WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (4th ed., 2017, incorporating the 1st and 2nd addenda) requires protection of drinking-water sources from cross-connection.
  • Wear nitrile gloves, chemical splash goggles, and a respirator rated for the specific chemical. Read the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) before opening any container.
  • Never mix concentrated acid with chlorine or with concentrated fertilizer. Add acid to water, never water to acid.
  • Flush the system with clean water for at least 15â20 minutes after fertigation before resuming normal irrigation.
  • Store chemicals in a locked, ventilated, labeled cabinet away from children, livestock, and food stores. Dispose of rinse water according to national regulations, not into drains or fields.
  • If a worker shows dizziness, vomiting, blurred vision, or skin burns, stop work, move to fresh air, remove contaminated clothing, and seek medical care immediately. Contact the nearest poison control centre.

Sources: WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (2017); FAO Safety and Health in Agriculture (2011); FAO Fertigation (2013).

How to use Table 2: Test the water source at least once per season, and immediately after any change in source, upstream activity, or flooding. If any parameter falls in the severe risk column, do not commission the system until treatment (filtration, acidification, chlorination, settling, or source change) is in place. For edible crops irrigated with water above WHO 2006 faecal coliform limits, switch to drip below the canopy, stop irrigation 1â2 days before harvest, and wash produce with safe water. Document every test result in the client file.

Quick Reference Checklist â Before You Leave the Site

  1. Source and safety: Confirm water source, backflow protection, and that no drinking-water point is downstream of any injection point.
  2. Pump and power: Record pump model, impeller size, voltage, current, and suction lift. Check for cavitation noise and vibration.
  3. Pressure: Measure pressure at the pump outlet, at the filter outlet, and at the farthest emitter. Compare to Table 1 design values.
  4. Flow: Measure actual flow at the block inlet and compare to design flow. Note any deviation greater than 10%.
  5. Filtration: Record filter type, mesh or media size, and pressure differential across the filter. Clean or backwash if differential exceeds 0.5 bar.
  6. Water quality: Record pH, EC, and any visible sediment, odour, or algae. Note whether a laboratory test is required against Table 2.
  7. Emitter performance: Sample at least 10 emitters per block. Record flow and check for clogging, leakage, or root intrusion.
  8. Client handover: Write the recommended flushing schedule, filter cleaning interval, and fertigation safety rules in the client's language. Sign and date the service record.

quiz.q: Which component in a drip irrigation system is primarily responsible for preventing debris from clogging emitters?
options: A) Pressure regulator
B) Filter
C) Backflow preventer
D) Air release valve
quiz.explanation: Filters trap sand, silt, and organic matter before water reaches the emitters, which is critical because drip emitters have very small openings.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a pressure regulator in an agricultural irrigation system?
options: A) To increase water pressure for long runs
B) To measure the total water volume used
C) To maintain a consistent downstream pressure
D) To inject fertilizer into the water line
quiz.explanation: Pressure regulators reduce and hold a steady downstream pressure so emitters and sprinklers operate within their designed range.

quiz.q: A technician measures 45 psi at the pump but only 12 psi at the last sprinkler on a zone. Which issue is most likely?
options: A) A clogged filter only
B) A faulty controller clock
C) Excessive friction loss in the piping
D) Too many emitters on the drip line
quiz.explanation: A large pressure drop between pump and the farthest outlet usually indicates friction loss from undersized pipe, long runs, or excessive fittings.

quiz.q: Which soil moisture sensor type measures water content by detecting the dielectric constant of the soil?
options: A) Tensiometer
B) Gypsum block
C) Granular matrix sensor
D) Capacitance probe
quiz.explanation: Capacitance probes use the soil dielectric constant to estimate volumetric water content and are common in modern irrigation scheduling.

quiz.q: When winterizing a drip irrigation system in a freezing climate, what is the recommended first step?
options: A) Shut off the water supply and drain the mainline
B) Add antifreeze to the drip tubing
C) Run the system at full pressure until it freezes
D) Remove all emitters and store them indoors
quiz.explanation: Shutting off the supply and draining the mainline removes standing water that could freeze and crack pipes, fittings, or valves.

quiz.q: Which factor most directly determines the precipitation rate of a sprinkler nozzle?
options: A) The color of the nozzle body
B) The nozzle flow rate and wetted area
C) The length of the lateral pipe
D) The type of controller used
quiz.explanation: Precipitation rate is calculated from the nozzle flow rate divided by the area it covers, so both flow and spacing matter.

quiz.q: A grower wants to apply 1 inch of water to a field using a system with a precipitation rate of 0.5 inches per hour. How long should the system run?
options: A) 30 minutes
B) 1 hour
C) 2 hours
D) 4 hours
quiz.explanation: At 0.5 inches per hour, applying 1 inch requires 1 divided by 0.5, which equals 2 hours of runtime.

quiz.q: Which practice best reduces the risk of runoff when irrigating a sloped field with a high application rate?
options: A) Increasing nozzle size to finish faster
B) Irrigating at midday for maximum evaporation
C) Removing all pressure regulators
D) Using cycle and soak scheduling
quiz.explanation: Cycle and soak scheduling splits runtime into shorter pulses so water infiltrates between cycles, reducing runoff on slopes or tight soils.
